name: Jiani (Elva) He
headline: Data Science Consultant · Independent Researcher
bio: Jiani (Elva) He is a data scientist and independent researcher based in Seattle, Washington. As a Data Science Consultant at Accenture, Jiani has spent five years applying analytics, optimization, and AI to forward and reverse logistics for a technology client. Jiani’s research asks how evidence becomes better operational decisions, spanning demand-forecast stability, causal decision support, trustworthy AI deployment, and AI-assisted reverse logistics. This work includes six 2026 papers with collaborators, among them a first-author paper accepted at AIBThings 2026, and Jiani has peer-reviewed more than ten journal manuscripts. Jiani holds an MS in Business Analytics from MIT (Operations Research Center) and a BS in Industrial Engineering from Purdue University.
highlights: First-author paper on semantic signals for reverse-logistics inspection, accepted at AIBThings 2026
Five more accepted conference papers with collaborators: IEOM 2026 (two papers), ICECCME 2026, ICEME 2026, and ICOAI 2026
National-priority research areas: AI for planning and decision making and AI assurance, both named as AI subfields on the U.S. Critical and Emerging Technologies List
MIT MS in Business Analytics (GPA 4.7/5.0) and Purdue BS in Industrial Engineering (Honors & Distinction, GPA 3.9/4.0)

streams.label: Forecasting & planning
streams.name: Forecasting & Planning Value
streams.question: When do better predictions actually produce better plans?
streams.motivation: A more accurate forecast is not automatically a better planning input. Forecasts that swing from one run to the next create churn in replenishment, and a new analytical capability creates value only if it changes the plans that are executed.
streams.practice: Analyzing demand, stock targets, and shortages for a technology client’s supply network

streams.label: Decision support & trustworthy AI
streams.name: Causal Decision Support & Trustworthy AI
streams.question: Which action should come next, and when can the evidence behind it be trusted?
streams.motivation: Detecting a disruption is not the same as knowing which intervention recovers the most value. Good decisions need causal evidence and explicit costs and delays. AI-enabled decisions also need provenance that people can review before deployment.
streams.practice: Rebalancing inventory across sites and standardizing enterprise LLM workflows

streams.label: Reverse logistics
streams.name: AI-Assisted Reverse Logistics
streams.question: How can unstructured signals guide inspection and recovery when labor is scarce?
streams.motivation: Returned assets arrive with uncertain condition and free-text notes. Choosing how deeply to inspect each one, and whether it goes to reuse, resale, recycling, or disposal, is a resource-allocation problem under partial information.
streams.practice: Tracking reverse-logistics cycle times and guiding asset-disposition decisions

publications.title: Semantic Signal-Assisted Inspection and Recovery Allocation in Reverse Logistics
publications.venue: 4th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Blockchain, and Internet of Things (AIBThings 2026)
publications.summary: Uses semantic signals in return notes to guide inspection depth and recovery allocation when asset condition is uncertain and inspection labor is limited. Evaluated in three synthetic reverse-logistics scenarios.
publications.short: Semantic-signal inspection and recovery allocation (first author)

publications.title: When Does an Added Planning Capability Create Operational Value? An Observable Evidence Standard
publications.venue: 3rd World Congress on Industrial Engineering and Operations Management · Irvine, California
publications.summary: An observable evidence standard for deciding whether an added planning capability changes executed plans and improves operational outcomes, evaluated through forecast-to-plan replay on retail datasets.
publications.short: Observable evidence standard for planning capabilities

publications.title: From Weak Signals to Supply Chain Reliability Risk: A Feedback-Driven Risk Accumulation Framework for Late-Delivery Prediction, Early Warning, and Risk Prioritization
publications.venue: 3rd World Congress on Industrial Engineering and Operations Management · Irvine, California
publications.record: Accepted manuscript · not yet publicly available
publications.summary: A leakage-controlled, feedback-driven risk-accumulation framework that turns weak operational signals into late-delivery predictions, early warnings, and cost-sensitive risk prioritization.
publications.short: Late-delivery risk prediction and early warning

publications.title: DACRI: Decision-Aware Causal Intervention Ranking for Critical Supply Chains
publications.venue: International Conference on Electrical, Computer, Communications and Mechatronics Engineering (ICECCME 2026) · 15–17 October 2026 · Bali, Indonesia
publications.summary: Ranks supply-chain interventions by recoverable net value, using a controlled synthetic benchmark with causal ground truth and explicit intervention costs, delays, and uncertainty. Identifies when adaptive ranking pays off and when simpler structural policies remain preferable.

publications.title: Accuracy-Preserving Stability Regularization for Large-Scale Retail Demand Forecasting
publications.summary: Training-time regularization that makes retail demand forecasts steadier from run to run while preserving point accuracy, evaluated on selected M5 demand series at multiple scales.

publications.title: Policy-Bounded, Provenance-Aware Deployment Assurance for LLM Request Routing
publications.summary: Studies how policy boundaries, provenance, and evidence identity determine whether an LLM request-routing package is qualified for deployment and for later updates.
publications.short: Deployment assurance for LLM request routing

importance.title: Decisions that keep critical systems running.
importance.lead: Supply chains and AI systems now sit underneath much of the economy. When a forecast swings without reason, a disruption is met with the wrong intervention, or an AI recommendation cannot be traced, the cost shows up as shortages, idle capacity, discarded hardware, and lost trust. My research asks how to make these decisions measurably better, and how to show that they are.

pillars.label: Supply-chain resilience
pillars.title: Acting on disruptions, not just detecting them
pillars.text: Disruptions in critical supply chains ripple into manufacturing, health care, and national security. Planners need to know which intervention recovers the most value when information is partial and delayed, and they need forecasts steady enough to plan around. DACRI ranks interventions by the net value they recover; my forecasting and late-delivery work aims to give planners earlier, steadier signals.

pillars.label: Trustworthy AI
pillars.title: Evidence that AI improves real decisions
pillars.text: As organizations bring AI into operational decisions, they need evidence that a new capability actually changes outcomes, and that its recommendations can be traced, reviewed, and governed before deployment. With collaborators, I have proposed an observable evidence standard for planning capabilities and a provenance-aware assurance framework for routing requests to large language models.

pillars.label: Recovering value
pillars.title: A second life for returned technology
pillars.text: Returned and retired electronics must be inspected and routed to reuse, resale, recycling, or disposal, usually with limited inspection labor. Better routing keeps usable hardware in service and recovers valuable materials instead of discarding them. My first-author paper shows how semantic signals in free-text return notes can direct inspection effort where it matters most.

philosophy.intro: Some of the most useful things I know, I learned from operations. Here are a few stories and principles that shape how I work and live.
philosophy.quote: The world has always had enough resources. The work is in using them well, and that is how I hope to help more people.

groups.title: What I try to live by.

items.title: Judge a model by the decision it changes.
items.text: It is easy to fall in love with a clever method. Before I commit to a research question, I ask: if this works completely, will a real decision get better? If not, I keep looking for a better question.

items.title: Say exactly what you know.
items.text: Evidence earns trust only when it is reported honestly: what was tested, what wasn’t, and how sure we are. I would rather make a smaller claim that holds than a bigger one that doesn’t.

items.title: Everything deserves a second life.
items.text: In reverse logistics, a returned device isn’t waste; it’s an asset whose next use hasn’t been decided yet. I try to treat setbacks the same way: inspect them honestly, keep what’s valuable, and route the rest toward something new.

items.title: Steady beats spectacular.
items.text: My forecasting research favors predictions that don’t swing wildly from week to week, because steadiness is what lets others plan. I try to be that kind of colleague and friend: consistent, reliable, and there when it counts.

stories.title: Why I chose optimization
text: I have always believed that the world has enough resources. What it often lacks is the ability to use them well and get them to the right place. That belief is why I chose to study operations research and optimization: at heart, they are the science of allocating what we have so that it helps more people.

I see the same pattern in my work today: inventory sitting at one site while another runs short, returned devices that could still be used, inspection hours spent where they matter least. Each one is a chance to do more with what already exists, and that is the kind of problem I want to spend my career on.

stories.title: Always learning
text: I am someone who always wants to keep improving. Since graduating, I have kept learning well beyond my field, from investing to a range of sports, because I want to grow as a whole person and not only as a professional.
I hope to keep growing in every direction for the rest of my life.

stories.title: Someone people can talk to
text: I think of myself as an energetic, warm person, and the people around me often come to me when they are facing a problem. Many times, after we talk, I see them leave a little lighter, and nothing makes me happier than that.
Whether I am mentoring a junior analyst or talking through a problem with a friend, being able to help is one of the things that makes my life feel meaningful.
